name: Nicotine (taken by mouth or through skin patches)
short: Case reports: death after massive patch and tablet exposure; respiratory failure after excess gum. Child poisonings from nicotine replacement products. Colitis trials: patches raised adverse events.
text: These data cover medicinal nicotine taken by mouth (capsules, gum, tablets) or through the skin as patches, not smoking. Poisoning can be fatal: a 2020 case report describes a 41-year-old man found dead with 7 nicotine patches on his body, with 14 nicotine patches and 5 empty blister packs of nicotine tablets in the bin, and lethal blood levels of nicotine and its breakdown product cotinine; the post-mortem examinations found asphyxia syndrome, and therapeutic levels of five other medicines (cyamemazine, lormetazepam, nordiazepam, oxazepam and buprenorphine) and signs of cannabis use were also found. The authors highlight the risk of nicotine poisoning in people using patches. In a 2022 case report, a 29-year-old man who chewed large numbers of nicotine gums over 4 days developed involuntary limb movements, then sudden loss of consciousness and respiratory failure needing a breathing tube and mechanical ventilation; he recovered and went home on the fifth day. Children: French poison control and toxicovigilance centres identified 318 cases of exposure to nicotine replacement products in children under 10 between 2000 and 2010; the exposure caused symptoms in 62 of them, about two-thirds of whom were under 4, and the abstract does not give their outcomes. The article reporting this describes the first signs of nicotine poisoning as gastrointestinal (vomiting, diarrhoea), cardiovascular (fast heart rate, high blood pressure) and neuropsychological (tremor of the extremities), and says that with higher doses these are rapidly followed by loss of consciousness, convulsions or respiratory failure; it states that in children poisoning can occur after ingestion of 1 mg of nicotine per kilogram of body weight, a dose it says is sometimes fatal in adults. It reports that most poisonings involving patches occur when a child finds an unused patch, or a used patch that an adult has thrown in a bin without proper precautions, and that some involve patches that have come off an adult's skin. In a prospective series from 34 US poison centres over 24 months, 36 children under 16 (mean age 3) were exposed to nicotine patches: 18 on the skin, and 18 who had bitten, chewed or swallowed part of a patch. Fourteen (39%) developed symptoms, including nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, weakness, dizziness or localised rashes; 10 were seen in an emergency department, 2 were admitted overnight, and all recovered fully. The authors report that these unintentional exposures usually involved used patches, were brief (under 20 minutes) and needed only skin decontamination and supportive care. In people with ulcerative colitis, a Cochrane review of 5 randomised trials found that patients on transdermal nicotine (skin patches) were more likely to have an adverse event (odds ratio 3.54) and to withdraw because of one (odds ratio 5.82) than those on placebo or standard treatment, and concluded that the adverse events are significant and limit its use in some patients. A 2021 review of 33 studies of non-smokers given patches for more than 48 hours (987 non-smokers in all, who received or did not receive nicotine) found nausea and skin itching the most common side effects; 43 (7.1%) stopped because of an adverse event and no hospital admissions for nicotine side effects were reported. Taken by mouth: in a pilot study in 8 never-smokers with primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC), side effects were frequent; three of five who completed a year had to lower the dose for a time, one stopped after four months because of dizziness and palpitations, and two stopped after one month because their colitis flared and needed corticosteroids. In an open-label study in 31 people with inflammatory bowel disease given oral nicotine capsules, 24 had nicotine-related non-serious adverse events and 7 stopped because of them, and 3 patients whose disease had been in remission developed active symptoms. With patches in PSC, in a 12-patient crossover trial one patient developed new ulcerative colitis and two did not finish because of bacterial cholangitis (bile-duct infection); the abstract does not say during which period these happened. In smokers trying to quit, a Cochrane review of nicotine replacement products reported skin irritation from patches and mouth irritation from gum and tablets, and higher odds of chest pain or palpitations (odds ratio 1.88), although these were rare and serious adverse events extremely rare; a review of 21 placebo-controlled trials found an increased risk of cardiac disorders, mainly palpitations, and in people at high cardiovascular risk 1.2% had a serious cardiovascular event, not significantly different from placebo. Pregnancy: a 2021 systematic review of nicotine replacement in pregnancy found non-significant estimates, compared with smoking, that pointed to possibly lower risks for several birth outcomes but possibly increased risks of miscarriage and stillbirth, with low or very low confidence, and concluded that the evidence does not show clearly whether it harms the fetus. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
